faq.a: High airway pressures can worsen pulmonary hypertension and cause barotrauma in hypoplastic lungs.
Only after the infant is stabilised; premature repair increases mortality.
faq.q: Can CDH be repaired immediately after birth?

faq.a: It selectively reduces pulmonary vascular resistance, improving oxygenation in pulmonary hypertension.
faq.q: What is the role of inhaled nitric oxide?

exam: What immediate steps do you take for a newborn with suspected CDH presenting in severe respiratory distress? — Secure airway, provide gentle ventilation with low pressures, obtain chest X‑ray, start inhaled nitric oxide if pulmonary hypertension suspected.
How does the observed‑to‑expected LHR influence counselling and management? — It predicts severity; low O/E LHR (<25 %) signals high mortality and may prompt early transfer to a tertiary centre.

A baby with left‑sided CDH has a scaphoid abdomen but normal chest X‑ray. What is your next investigation? — Perform a bedside ultrasound to look for intrathoracic bowel loops; a normal X‑ray can miss small defects.
Why is eventration of the diaphragm not managed the same way as CDH? — Eventration has an intact diaphragm; it usually does not cause pulmonary hypoplasia, so surgery is rarely needed.

What are the contraindicated ventilation strategies in CDH and why? — High‑frequency oscillatory ventilation with excessive mean airway pressure can worsen pulmonary hypertension and should be avoided unless other measures fail.

Explain the rationale for delaying surgical repair in CDH. — Stabilisation reduces peri‑operative mortality; repairing a severely hypoxic infant increases risk of cardiac arrest and postoperative respiratory failure.

Which associated cardiac anomaly most commonly co‑exists with CDH and how does it affect management? — Ventricular septal defect; it may exacerbate pulmonary hypertension and requires echocardiographic assessment before surgery.

How would you counsel parents about recurrence risk after an isolated CDH? — Recurrence is low (~1 %); advise prenatal ultrasound in future pregnancies and discuss genetic counseling if a syndrome is identified.
ai.title: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia
related: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A life‑threatening birth defect where abdominal viscera herniate into the thorax through a diaphragmatic defect, most often left‑sided, causing pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory distress. Early recognition, stabilisation and timely surgery improve survival, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Usually left posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect
May be diagnosed prenatally by ultrasound or postnatally by clinical signs
sections.p: A congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a defect in the diaphragm that allows abdominal organs to migrate into the chest cavity, impairing lung development and function.

b: Mild: O/E LHR ≥ 45 % or requires < 40 % FiO₂
Moderate: O/E LHR 25‑44 % or needs 40‑60 % FiO₂
Severe: O/E LHR < 25 % or requires > 60 % FiO₂, high‑frequency ventilation, or ECMO
sections.p: Severity is graded by the observed‑to‑expected lung‑to‑head ratio (O/E LHR) on prenatal ultrasound and by postnatal respiratory support needs.

b: Isolated sporadic defect (most common)
Associated genetic syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome, chromosomal deletions)
Heterotaxy or other laterality disorders
Maternal exposures (smoking, certain medications) – less common in low‑resource settings
sections.p: CDH results from failure of the pleuroperitoneal membranes to close during weeks 4‑8 of gestation.

b: Tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring
Cyanosis despite oxygen
Scaphoid (sunken) abdomen, bowel sounds in chest
Mediastinal shift on chest X‑ray
sections.p: Newborns present with respiratory distress soon after birth; the degree of distress correlates with lung hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.

t.b: Confirms defect and estimates lung size; guides counselling and delivery planning
Shows bowel loops in thorax and mediastinal shift; confirms diagnosis when ultrasound unavailable
Assesses pulmonary hypertension and associated cardiac anomalies; essential before surgery
Evaluates oxygenation and ventilation; guides need for ventilation strategies
Prepares for possible transfusion during repair

b: Refractory hypoxemia despite maximal ventilation
Severe pulmonary hypertension on echo
Abdominal organ ischemia (e.g., strangulated bowel)
Post‑operative diaphragmatic recurrence
sections.p: Complications arise from severe pulmonary hypoplasia, persistent pulmonary hypertension, and abdominal organ compromise.

b: Gentle ventilation (avoid high pressures) – reduces barotrauma
Sedation and paralysis only if needed for ventilation
Inhaled nitric oxide for pulmonary hypertension
Delayed surgical repair (usually within 24‑72 h) after stabilisation
Surgical approach: open or minimally invasive patch repair; use non‑absorbable sutures
Avoid routine prophylactic antibiotics unless infection suspected
sections.p: Stabilise the airway and circulation first, then repair the defect when the infant is physiologically stable.

b: Regular pulmonary function testing
Growth monitoring and feeding support
Neurodevelopmental screening at 6‑month intervals
Counselling families about recurrence risk (≈1 % for siblings)
sections.p: Long‑term follow‑up focuses on respiratory, nutritional and neurodevelopmental outcomes.

b: Eventration of diaphragm – intact diaphragm, elevated but functional
Mediastinal mass – solid lesion, no bowel loops on X‑ray
Congenital pulmonary airway malformation – cystic lung lesions, not abdominal viscera
sections.p: Conditions that also cause bowel sounds in the chest or respiratory distress in newborns.

b: Normal chest X‑ray early if herniated organs are small; repeat if suspicion remains
ABG may show acceptable PaO₂ with high FiO₂; look at PaCO₂ and oxygen index
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite severe disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of abdominal organ compromise (abdominal distension, absent stool passage)
